How does an egg turn into a cloud of meringue?

A slippery egg white becomes a mound of foam. Follow the tiny bubbles inside a meringue and discover what the whisk is really doing.

By Biel Sardà · Published 9 Oct 2026 · Suggest a correction

A bowl full of air

Crack an egg and the white slips into the bowl, barely holding a shape. Pick up a whisk and, a few minutes later, it can stand in glossy peaks. Where did all that extra stuff come from?

Much of the new volume is air. Beating egg whites traps bubbles inside a network of proteins. Add sugar and bake according to a meringue recipe, and that fragile foam can become a dessert you can pick up.

If you have admired a Mary Berry pavlova, you have already seen the result: a crisp shell with a softer centre, strong enough to carry cream and fruit. The surprising part happens before the toppings arrive.

The whisk has two jobs

A whisk pushes air into the liquid, but air alone would not explain why the bubbles stay. The egg white also contains folded protein molecules. At the boundary between air and water, those molecules rearrange.

Some parts of a protein are drawn to water; others turn towards the air. As the proteins unfold and connect, they form a thin network around the bubbles. Picture lots of tiny rooms being built while the whisk keeps adding more guests.

The Exploratorium describes this change in the proteins as denaturation. You do not need to remember the word to spot the effect: the mixture begins to hold a shape instead of immediately flowing flat.

Why the oven matters

The oven gives the foam its next transformation. As the trapped air warms, it expands, while the surrounding protein network sets. Handled well, the structure can remain after the bubbles themselves stop doing the work. The Exploratorium’s egg-science guide follows that journey from whisk to heat.

That is why making a meringue involves more than simply stirring sweetness into an egg. You are building a structure, then helping it keep its shape.

The details still matter. Berry’s pavlova recipe specifies gradual additions of sugar and a cooling stage in the switched-off oven. Follow a complete recipe for those steps; understanding the bubbles explains the trick, but it does not replace the method.

Next time you see a whisk

Watch the mixture rather than just the clock. The liquid, the foam and the finished dessert began with the same ordinary ingredient. What changed was the arrangement—and how much air it could hold.

An egg looks like a very small starting point for a cloud. A bowl, a whisk and a little chemistry make it less mysterious.
